source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers? (ISSTA)
finding: Full text opened. Students used a Tarantula ranked-statement list in Eclipse. The tool did not make them faster on average. Only the best performers on the easy task gained.
numbers: 34 students in the first run (design check), then 24 students in the main run (groups A and B) and 10 more in a rank-change follow-up (groups C and D). 30 minutes per task. Tetris (easy; 2 of 10 recorded runs hit the fault): mean 12:42 with tool vs 14:14 without, not significant. NanoXML (harder): 20:16 vs 22:30, not significant. High performers only (N=10): 8:51 with tool vs 14:28 without, p<0.05, two-tailed t-test. Finished tasks: 18 on Tetris vs 10 on NanoXML. Ratio of Tetris to NanoXML time differed by group (2.5x vs 1.3x, p<0.02), so no extra help on the harder task.
quote: The rank of the faulty statement may not be as important as other factors or strategies
limits: Two bugs only (6,811 LOC in total). One old formula (Tarantula). Students. Group labels A and B swap between tasks in the paper, so tool and no-tool arms must be read per task. The first run was used to fix flaws, so the main result is a second sample.
agent_relevance: A ranked suspicious list gave no mean gain to people who still had to understand the bug. Do not expect a spectrum to lift an agent that already reads the failing test well.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) rank-change follow-up and navigation logs
finding: Moving the faulty line far up or down the list did not change time. People did not read the list in order and did not stop when they saw the fault.
numbers: Group C kept the true rank; group D had it changed. Tetris fault moved from rank 7 to 35: 10:12 (C) vs 12:36 (D). NanoXML fault moved from 83 to 16: 15:12 (C) vs 18:30 (D); D was slower despite the better rank. Neither difference significant; Tetris/NanoXML time ratio 0.79 in both groups. N=5 per group. Logs from 22 usable of 24: 37% of visits jumped more than one position, average jump 10 positions, 10.3 direction changes (zigzags) per person (range 1 to 36). Of 10 people who clicked the fault, only 1 stopped; on average 61% of tool time came after first seeing the fault (about ten more minutes).
limits: Tiny groups (5 per arm), so the null is weak evidence. Xia et al. 2016 argue the rank change was between two bad ranks (83 to 16), so no effect is expected there.
agent_relevance: Seeing the faulty line is not the same as understanding it. For the agent, the next step after a hit must be an explanation check, not an immediate stop or an immediate patch.

source: Xia, Bao, Lo, Li (2016) Automated debugging considered harmful considered harmful: a user study with professionals (ICSME)
finding: Full text opened. With professionals, real bugs and a top-10 list, the ranked list made them clearly faster and more successful. The effect was larger when the fault sat in the top 5 than in places 6 to 10.
numbers: 36 professionals (3 to 4 years experience, 2 companies in China), 12 per group, 16 real Defects4J bugs from 4 projects, each person fixed 4 bugs, 3 hours per 4 bugs, about 80 recorded hours. Accurate tool (fault put at random in ranks 1 to 5): success 98% (47/48), mean 11.38 min. Mediocre tool (ranks 6 to 10): 94% (45/48), 16.35 min. No tool (Eclipse debugger): 77% (37/48), 26.45 min. Accurate vs none: Wilcoxon p=1.306e-10, Cliff's delta 0.8012 (large). Mediocre vs none: p=1.024e-5, delta 0.5456 (large). Accurate vs mediocre: p=0.0015, delta 0.3589 (medium). 9 of 12 mediocre-tool users called it useful, 3 did not.
quote: fault localization can positively impact debugging success and efficiency
limits: The tool was simulated: the real fault was placed at a random rank inside the band and the other entries came from the execution trace. Only the top 10 were shown. Single-fault bugs, bugs picked for medium difficulty. Time for failed fixes was dropped (survivor effect). 12 people per group. Not a real SBFL formula.
agent_relevance: A reliable hint inside the top 5 roughly halves human debugging time. A hint outside the top 5 still helps but less. This is the human upper bound for a hint that is correct.

source: Xia et al. (2016) navigation behaviour and why it conflicts with Parnin and Orso
finding: People read the first few entries in order, then sampled at random. They used the list to make hypotheses to check with breakpoints, and trusted it only if it looked right in the first five entries.
numbers: 23 of 24 tool users used it the same way (open top items, set breakpoints, read variable values, re-check list). 20 of 24 (83.3%) read the top 5 in order; 18 of 24 (75%) read through rank 5, but only 8 (33.3%) read through rank 6, and 3 (12.5%) through rank 8. A user said: 'I only trust the top-5 statements'. Authors explain the conflict with Parnin and Orso by (a) professionals not students, (b) 16 bugs not 2, (c) larger code, (d) rank changes of 83 to 16 and 7 to 35 are bad-to-bad or fair-to-bad moves, and 5 vs 5 data points cannot reach significance.
limits: The explanation is the authors' reading, not a replication. Self-reported comments are from a small group. The fault was always in the top 10, so no case of a fully wrong list was tested.
agent_relevance: Resolves gap 9 in part: the two studies differ in population, tool realism and task size, so they do not directly contradict. A hint list is useful as a source of hypotheses to test with probes, and only the top few items get attention.

source: Xie, Liu, Song, Chen, Xuan, Xu (2016) Revisit of automatic debugging via human focus-tracking analysis (ICSE companion)
finding: Not opened: the ACM copy is closed access (Unpaywall: oa_status closed). Only seen through how Xia et al. describe it. It is said to find that SBFL can weaken programmers' fault detection when the tool mismatches what they need.
numbers: Per Xia et al.: 17 debugging tasks, synthetic bugs injected into 7 toy programs of 17 to 500 lines, 3rd-year college students, an Ochiai-based tool. The N=207 figure from an earlier search snippet could not be checked and is NOT confirmed.
limits: Second-hand description by a paper that disagrees with it. Participant count and effect sizes unverified. Gap 9 stays open for Xie.
agent_relevance: Treat the 'SBFL harms people' result as unverified toy-program evidence. Do not rest an agent design on it.

source: Zhang, Ruan, Fan, Roychoudhury (2024) AutoCodeRover (ISSTA): SBFL ablation, RQ2
finding: Giving the agent the top-5 SBFL methods at the start of context search raised SWE-bench Lite resolution a little at almost the same token cost. The agent did not just follow rank 1.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, 300 tasks, GPT-4 era model. Without SBFL: 19.00% (57 resolved), 37k tokens ($0.43) per task. With SBFL (ACR-sbfl): 22.00% (66), 40k tokens ($0.47), 250 s. ACR with 3 runs: 26.00% (78), 112k tokens. ACR-sbfl uniquely solved 7 tasks no other run solved. Case django-13964: the agent skipped the rank-1 method and searched ranks 3 and 5 because they matched clues in the issue text.
limits: One run per arm, so the 9-task gain is inside run-to-run noise (best of 3 reached 78). SBFL used the developer-written tests of each task, which include the tests the fix must pass, so test quality is better than in real use. The comparison arm had no test information at all, not the failing-test output alone.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for gap 1: about +8% tokens for +3 points, but not shown above noise. A hint list is read together with the issue text, not obeyed blindly.

source: Shi, Yang, Chen (2026) From Finding to Fixing: How useful is fault localization for agentic program repair? (arXiv 2610.25826), RQ1
finding: Six recent LLM-based FL methods plugged into one agent (mini-swe-agent) did not raise repair success. Pass@1 fell in 17 of 18 settings. Even gold locations only help by a few points.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified (500) and Defects4J v3.0.1; repair models GPT-5.6 Luna, DeepSeek-v4 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite; 16,248 trajectories. Change in pass@1 from -4.45 to +0.40 points; only gain +0.40 (Gemini with CoSIL). Example: GPT-5.6 Luna no-FL 73.4%, with LocAgent 72.0%, CoSIL 72.0%, OrcaLoca 71.2%; LocAgent gave 16 gains vs 23 losses. McNemar: 16 of 18 settings p>=0.05; two significant drops (p=0.036, p=0.006) vanish after Holm correction (0.607, 0.107). Gold locations: +0.8 to +4.6 points pass@1 over no-FL across original issues, LR-issues, Multimodal and Pro.
limits: The six FL methods are LLM-based, issue-based or failing-test-based, not plain Ochiai hints, though several use coverage inside. SWE-bench issues already contain location clues. Cheaper 'Flash' models for repair. One agent harness.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent evidence for gap 2: for a strong agent that can search the repo, a location hint is worth at most a few points even if perfect. Expect a spectrum hint to be a token saver at best, not an accuracy gain.

source: Shi et al. (2026) From Finding to Fixing, RQ2: anchoring on misleading localisation
finding: When none of the suggested files was correct, agents often looked at them first but many then reached a correct file anyway. Recovery was weakest for the smallest model.
numbers: Cases with completely misleading file-level guidance: 7 to 206 per setting. Initial anchoring (first inspection includes a suggested file): 34.5% to 100.0%. Recovery among anchored runs: 34.8% to 95.9%; over half recovered in 13 of 18 settings; below 50% in all three Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Defects4J settings. Initial inspection of FL-recommended files 86.0% to 100.0% with FL. Manual study: 29 anchored wrong-FL cases, 16 later reached a gold file; of 40 wrong-FL runs, 23 kept their main edit in the suggested code (9 passed) and 17 moved elsewhere (13 passed).
limits: Counts files, not lines. Anchoring is measured from first inspected file only. FL lists come from LLM methods, not from a collapsed coverage spectrum. Nothing was tested on a ranked list with confident scores that is wrong.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 3 for strong models in the repair setting: anchoring is real (up to 100%) but recovery is usual with a capable model and poor with a small one. Our S5 should add a 'hint disagreed with evidence' check.

source: Shi et al. (2026) From Finding to Fixing, RQ2.4: tokens and cost of localisation
finding: A location hint makes the repair shorter, but producing the hint often costs more tokens than it saves.
numbers: Repair-stage tokens: down in 16 of 18 settings (from -31.3% to +9.8%); steps down in 17 settings (-23.5% to +0.2%). End-to-end tokens including FL: up in 13 settings, down in 5 (range -16.4% to +129.8%); all six GPT-5.6 Luna settings went up. Gold symbols cut repair tokens by up to 39.2% (LR-issue: 113.7K, -39.2%). FL mainly shortens the first-reach step (by 0.11 to 2.04 steps); gold-file reach was already 88.6% to 99.4% without FL.
limits: Cost counted in tokens, not dollars. Spectrum collection (running tests) is not token cost and is not counted here.
agent_relevance: At equal tokens a hint must be nearly free to win. A spectrum from tests the agent already ran costs no model tokens, so it is a better bet than an LLM-made hint.

source: Rafi and Chen (2026) Order Matters: LLM input-order bias in fault localization (ICSE 26, arXiv 2412.18750), RQ4 ordering strategies
finding: Putting methods in Ochiai order helped GPT-4o-mini a lot over bare Ochiai, but did no better than ordering by plain code size or by call-graph distance to the failing test.
numbers: Defects4J, 501 faults, method-level, gpt-4o-mini. Ochiai alone: Top-1 101. LLM given the list in Ochiai order: 164 (32.7%). Metric-based order (LOC): about 163 (32.5%). CallGraphBFS from the failing test: 175 (34.9%). CallGraphDFS: 173 (34.5%). Learned DepGraph order: 242 (48.3%). Order bias: perfect vs worst order at segment size 50: 278 (55.5%) vs 170 (33.9%) Top-1; at segment size 10 about 41.5% vs 39.3%.
limits: Table text is partly garbled by PDF extraction, so the LOC row is read from the layout and the paper's remark that LOC and Ochiai are within 0.2 points at Top-1. Single weak model. This is the order of a candidate list, not a separate hint block.
agent_relevance: Closest equal-token test for gaps 1 and 4: the same candidate set, only the order changes. A spectrum order is no better than a trivial order, so the value of the spectrum lies in which lines are covered, not in the scores.

source: Rafi and Chen (2026) Order Matters: renaming check for memorisation
finding: Renaming methods cut Top-1 by 4 to 9%, so some Defects4J answers come from memory, but order bias is not explained by memory. Leakage rates are quoted from LessLeak-Bench.
numbers: Segment size 10: Top-1 217 to 208 (-4%) after renaming; segment size 50: 278 to 253 (-9%). Renamed worst-order run: 152 bugs (30.3%) vs perfect order 253 (50.5%). LessLeak-Bench rates as quoted by the authors: 0.41% leakage for Defects4J, 11% for BugsInPy.
limits: Renaming does not remove memory of code bodies. LessLeak figures are second-hand here. Only gpt-4o-mini and DeepSeek.
agent_relevance: For gap 8: a few points of the Defects4J LLM score may be memory. The check should be repeated on fresh bugs for our own tests.

source: Yang et al. (2024) LLMAO (ICSE 24): baseline granularity check
finding: The Ochiai Top-1 of 19 in LLMAO is a statement-level number on Defects4J 1.2 (395 bugs), with DeepFL tie handling. The Ochiai figure of 80 in AgentFL-style tables is method-level. They are not in conflict.
numbers: LLMAO Table 2, Defects4J v1.2.0, statement level: Ochiai Top-1/3/5 = 19 (4.8%) / 65 (16.5%) / 99 (25.1%); DeepFL 57; DeepRL4FL 71; TRANSFER-FL 86; LLMAO CodeGen-350M 82, 6B 85, 16B 88 (22.3%).
limits: Different granularity and tie rule from the method-level tables. This closes the 19-vs-80 discrepancy (K19) by granularity, not by an error in either paper.
agent_relevance: Always say statement or method when quoting Top-1. For an agent, method-level is the cheaper hint and probably the natural unit.

source: Farzandway and Ghassemi (2026) SieveFL (arXiv 2605.13491): coverage as a filter before the LLM
finding: Using failing-test coverage only to drop never-executed methods (not to rank) cut candidates by 79% and input tokens by about 49% with Top-1 unchanged. A small open model reached the AgentFL level.
numbers: 395 Defects4J v1.2 bugs, method level, Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B on a commodity PC. SieveFL Top-1 165 (41.8%), MRR 0.469, +2.1 points over AgentFL (157). Paired on 383 bugs: mean candidates 398.8 to 187.2; wall-clock 5.07 to 4.05 min; Top-3 to Top-10 up 2.3 to 2.4 points. Coverage-only scoring (no semantic signal) lost 0.5 points Top-1, 2.7 Top-3, 3.2 Top-5, 3.5 Top-10. Table (from original papers): Ochiai method-level Top-1 80, AgentFL 157, DeepFL 176, GRACE 192. Closure: coverage footprints too similar, LLM screening less useful.
limits: Uses failing-test coverage only, no passing tests, so this is a trace filter, not a spectrum. 12 incomplete runs counted as failures. Single model. GRACE (trained) still beats it overall.
agent_relevance: Direct support for using coverage to shrink the search space at equal or lower tokens (gap 1), and a warning that where tests share coverage the filter does little (gap 3).

source: Yang, Zhu, Zhang, Gupta, Kundu (2026) SemLoc (arXiv 2603.29109): coverage collapse and what an LLM does with tests
finding: On 809 real Python bugs, plain spectra fail often (the faulty line shares coverage with passing runs), but an LLM that is simply given the tests and errors does as well as the full SemLoc pipeline.
numbers: SemBugs, 809 bugs, 750 projects. SBFL misses first rank in at least 83.8% with each of six formulas; in 185 programs (22.9%) the faulty line ties with at least half of covered lines. On that coverage-collapse subset Ochiai Acc@1 is about 2.2% and misses the top five in 55.1%; SemLoc violations rank it first in 40.9% (alone) and 86.3% (full). Direct LLM seeing only the function: 50.0% Acc@1. LLM given the function, SSA form, passing tests and failing tests with errors (no coverage): 82.0% vs SemLoc 81.4%, not significant for any of four models (GPT-5.5, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.8-Flash). Acc@5 96.0% vs 93.4%. QuixBugs: Ochiai Acc@1 24.2%.
limits: No condition adds an Ochiai hint to the LLM, so SemLoc does not test gap 1 itself. Python, one-function scope, LLM-authored harnesses. Test pass/fail contents are what lifts the LLM from 50 to 82.
agent_relevance: The failing-test output carries most of the signal (50 to 82%). A spectrum hint has to beat that baseline, not no information. Where coverage collapses, the spectrum is empty and only values help.

source: Yang et al. (2026) SemLoc: wrong top answers, verification and cost
finding: Checking an LLM's top line by patching it and re-running tests separates right from wrong answers better than the LLM's own confidence, at 2 to 3 times the tokens. Half the value-check evidence comes from wrong checks.
numbers: When the top line is correct, the patch check verifies it in 76.9% of 7,845 runs; when wrong, in 19.9% of 1,836 runs (58.3% flagged irrelevant). 68.4% of top-1 answers verified; 93.6% of those correct. LLM confidence >=0.9 on 76.2% of answers, only 84.1% of those right; only 33.1% of wrong answers fall below the threshold. Of constraints violated by failing tests, 48.1% state intended behaviour and 51.9% do not. Cost 2.13 to 2.31 LLM calls, 2.2 to 3.0 times the tokens of a single call, about 3 s of test time, 3.3 to 3.7 test reruns per program. Wrong top lines that still pass the check: 366.
limits: Tests are the only oracle; a wrong line can pass. Fixes in the benchmark are one-line style. Tokens counted, not money.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: value-based spectra add cost (2 to 3 times tokens) and gave no top-1 gain over the plain LLM with the same inputs. For an agent that can print variables, the cheaper path is a probe plus a patch-and-rerun check.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which agent causes task failures and when? Who&When (ICML, arXiv 2505.00212)
finding: Non-code analogue: finding the step that broke a multi-step LLM run is hard even for o1 and R1 when the model reads one failure log. No spectrum over several attempts was tried.
numbers: 127 multi-agent systems, failure logs with agent and decisive-step labels. Best method: 53.5% agent-level, 14.2% step-level. Hand-crafted systems with ground truth: all-at-once agent 55.17% / step 5.26%; step-by-step 34.48% / 7.02%; binary search 51.72% / 6.90%; random 12.00% / 4.16%. Hybrid method: 57.02% agent / 12.28% step at 149,177 tokens vs 17,106 for all-at-once. Some methods below random.
limits: Single-trace blame, no pass/fail contrast across attempts, so it is not SBFL. Failure types are agent tool failures, not math errors.
agent_relevance: For gap 6: step blame from one attempt is near random at step level. A spectrum across many attempts of the same problem is a different, untested idea; this paper is the baseline to beat.

source: Sepidband, Pham, Hemmati (2026) On the role of fault localization context for LLM-based program repair (arXiv 2604.05481)
finding: Hint grain matters. File-level context gives large gains; adding line-level context often lowers repair success because of noise.
numbers: GPT-5-mini, 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, 61 context configurations. File-level localisation 15 to 17 times better than no file; best around 6 to 10 relevant files; line-level expansion frequently degrades results.
limits: One model, one benchmark. Context is code shown to the repair model, not a ranked suspiciousness list. Figures from the earlier c11 reading; the PDF was re-downloaded but only skimmed this session.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: for the form of the hint, coarse (file or function) beats line-level lists for a repair model. Give the agent functions, not a ranked list of 10 lines.

source: SA-BCL (Du et al.) as described in SieveFL (2026): multi-fault spectra
finding: Only classic SBFL work covers multi-fault localisation. SieveFL's related-work text reports that learning-based SA-BCL beats FLITSR on multi-fault Defects4J. No LLM-plus-FLITSR study was found.
numbers: As quoted in SieveFL: SA-BCL beats FLITSR by up to 37.5% in average wasted effort and 29.2% in precision on the TCM synthetic and Defects4J multi-fault sets. Causes named: few failing tests and noise when one fault hides another so some failing runs look like passing ones.
limits: Second-hand text; the SA-BCL paper (ACM TOIT) was not opened. Nothing about LLMs in the loop.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open. For our S5, the practical analogue is one-fix-then-retest, but no evidence says how many rounds before the spectrum is useless.
